analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA methane limits on new oil and gas facilities until a small-well study is finished.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by one sponsor and 10 Republican cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the EPA from finalizing any rule that tightens methane limits on new or modified oil and gas facilities until the Department of Energy finishes a study of methane emissions from small 'marginal' wells and opens at least 90 days for public comment on how to use the results. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and the rules being delayed were the Clean Air Act standards for leaks and vents at new drilling sites. The bill never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas operators, and especially small 'marginal' well producers, would benefit: the standards that limit methane leaks at new and modified facilities could not be finalized until the study and comment period were complete, postponing compliance costs. The bill directs the EPA to weigh the study's findings when it does finalize a rule, which operators could expect to shape the standards in their favor.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA from finalizing any Clean Air Act rule amending the new source performance standards (including subpart OOOOa) to reduce methane emissions from new and modified oil and natural gas facilities until the Energy Department completes and publishes its marginal well study.

Requires the Energy Department to provide at least 90 days for public comment on applying the study's results, and directs the EPA to take the study's findings into account when finalizing any methane rule.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on people living near oil and gas development and on the public generally, since finalizing methane limits for new and modified facilities would be postponed, extending emissions of a potent greenhouse gas. No offsetting benefit for the public is specified in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near drilling sites and the public

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith case for the bill: emissions from small marginal wells are poorly measured, and supporters argued the EPA should not set standards for those wells without data on what they actually emit [S3]. A delay to gather and publish such data is not inherently unreasonable.
The bill sets no deadline for the study or the comment period, so the delay it imposes on methane rules could be open-ended, and it conditions the EPA's authority on action by a different department.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose is to base standards on better data about small wells, which is a legitimate research goal. But the mechanism is a blank-check delay: no deadline for the study, and no methane standards for new facilities until it is done. The benefit is better data someday; the cost is postponing leak controls on new drilling sites indefinitely, with the burden falling on nearby residents and the climate rather than on operators.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, and it never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 17, 2021 by Rep. Jodey Arrington with 10 Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change, where no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the committee or the House ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the EPA kept the ability to finalize methane standards for new oil and gas facilities without first completing the marginal well study, and operators did not obtain the postponement the bill would have given them.

for.name: Rep. Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block EPA methane rules until the marginal well study is completed.

sides.party_line_note: All identified support came from Republicans — one sponsor and 10 cosponsors, all R — and no Democrat supported it; no floor vote ever occurred to test party splits.

industries.industry: Oil and gas operators (especially small marginal-well producers)
industries.note: The bill would delay methane limits on new and modified facilities until a study of small-well emissions was finished and a 90-day comment period ran, postponing the operators' compliance costs. The cost of that delay falls on nearby residents and the public through prolonged methane emissions.
